title: The Yeast Protein That Holds Three Kinases

scenes.tts: Yeast cells mate with three kinases in a row. Stee eleven switches on Stee seven, and Stee seven switches on Fus three. But Stee eleven also starts the cascade for too much salt, and the one for growing in long filaments. One enzyme, three destinations.
scenes.caption: Yeast cells mate with three kinases in a row. Ste11 switches on Ste7, and Ste7 switches on Fus3. But Ste11 also starts the cascade for too much salt, and the one for growing in long filaments. One enzyme, three destinations.
scenes.visual: Ste11, Ste7, Fus3 in a row to a mating response; Ste11 also sends arrows to a high-salt cascade and a filament cascade; the three destinations are lit.
scenes.narration: Yeast cells mate with three kinases in a row. Ste11 switches on Ste7, and Ste7 switches on Fus3. But Ste11 also starts the cascade for too much salt, and the one for growing in long filaments. One enzyme, three destinations.

scenes.tts: Elaine Elion's laboratory was working out which parts of a yeast protein three enzymes stuck to. The protein was Stee five. Without it, a yeast cell cannot mate. Yet Stee five had no enzyme activity. It never put a phosphate on anything, or took one off. In 1994, that came close to saying it had no mechanism.

scenes.visual: Three kinases hover above a long bar; question marks mark where each sticks. The bar is named Ste5, no Ste5 means no mating, a crossed-out phosphate shows no enzyme activity, and the question 'no mechanism?' closes the scene.

scenes.tts: Choi, Satterberg, Lyons and Elion reported that Stee eleven, Stee seven and Fus three bind different regions of Stee five. So one Stee five molecule can hold all three at once. Two other laboratories reached the same result that year, Michael Wigler's and George Sprague's.

scenes.visual: Each kinase has a peg of a different width and drops into its own slot on Ste5; all three sit on the one bar. Credit cards for the Cell paper, then Wigler (PNAS) and Sprague (Genetics).

scenes.tts: A scaffold buys speed. A kinase and its target normally find each other by drifting at random. On one scaffold they are already touching. It also buys insulation. The Stee eleven that a pheromone switches on sits against Fus three, steered away from the kinase that would tell the cell it was drying out. A protein that catalyzes nothing earns its place by what it buys the cell.

scenes.visual: Speed: a free kinase and target drift apart; on a scaffold they touch. Insulation: pheromone switches on Ste11 beside Fus3 on Ste5; a drying-out kinase is far away. Close: speed and insulation chips under a bar that catalyzes nothing.
